name: North-South to Kimura
description: Master North-South to Kimura transition in BJJ. Step-by-step arm isolation and control from dominant position. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 70%.
overview: The North-South to Kimura transition represents a fundamental attacking sequence from one of BJJ's most dominant control positions. From North-South position, the practitioner isolates the opponent's arm and transitions to the Kimura Trap control position, threatening a high-percentage shoulder lock submission. This technique capitalizes on the superior weight distribution and control inherent to the North-South position, where the opponent's defensive frames are compromised and their shoulders are vulnerable to attack. The transition requires precise timing and grip control, as the practitioner must maintain chest-to-chest pressure while manipulating the opponent's arm into the characteristic figure-four Kimura grip. Once established, the Kimura Trap offers multiple finishing options, sweep opportunities, and transitions to other dominant positions, making this a versatile and essential technique for any top game specialist. The position's effectiveness stems from the mechanical advantage created by controlling the opponent's shoulder joint while their mobility is restricted by your body weight.
key_principles: Maintain constant chest-to-chest pressure throughout the transition to prevent opponent escape
Control the near-side arm first before attempting to secure the Kimura grip
Use your head position to block the opponent's hip escape and maintain superior position
Secure the figure-four grip with proper hand placement: palm-to-palm connection
Keep your elbows tight to your body to maximize leverage on the shoulder joint
Transition your weight distribution smoothly to prevent the opponent from bridging or turning
Create the angle necessary for finishing by shifting your hips perpendicular to opponent's body
setup_requirements: Established North-South position with chest-to-chest pressure
Opponent's near-side arm is exposed or defending against your weight
Your head is positioned on the mat beside opponent's hip to block escape
Strong base with knees wide and weight distributed across opponent's chest
Opponent's far-side arm is controlled or pinned to prevent framing
Sufficient space to isolate and manipulate the near-side arm without losing position

execution_steps.description: Establish dominant North-South position with your chest pressing firmly into opponent's chest. Your head should be positioned low, near their far hip, with your arms wrapped around their torso or controlling their arms. Distribute your weight evenly with knees wide for maximum base and control.

Slide your near-side hand under the opponent's near-side arm, reaching for their wrist or forearm. Use your chest pressure to pin their arm against their body, preventing them from pulling it back to safety. Your far-side arm continues to control their far shoulder or head to maintain position.
execution_steps.timing: As opponent attempts to frame or push

execution_steps.description: Pull the opponent's wrist across their own body using your near-side hand, positioning their arm so the back of their hand is against their far shoulder or neck. This creates the necessary angle for the Kimura grip. Maintain downward pressure with your chest to prevent them from recovering their arm.

Reach your far-side hand over the opponent's arm and grab your own near-side wrist, creating the characteristic figure-four Kimura grip. Your near-side hand should have a firm grip on their wrist with thumb pointing toward their head. Ensure your elbows are tight and the grip is secure before proceeding.

Shift your hips toward the opponent's head while maintaining the Kimura grip, creating a perpendicular angle to their body. Walk your knees up toward their head to increase shoulder pressure. Your head should now be positioned near their far hip, blocking any hip escape attempts.

Sit back slightly, pulling the opponent's arm away from their body while maintaining the figure-four grip. Your chest should remain heavy on their upper body. From this Kimura Trap position, you can finish the submission by lifting their elbow while pulling their wrist toward their head, or transition to other attacks and positions.

common_counters.counter: Opponent grabs their own belt or gi to prevent arm isolation
common_counters.your_response: Attack the far-side arm with a choke or armbar to force them to release their defensive grip, then return to the Kimura attack

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges explosively to disrupt your base
common_counters.your_response: Widen your base, lower your center of gravity, and use your head to post on the mat. Ride out the bridge and re-establish control as they return to the mat

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns into you to recover guard
common_counters.your_response: Follow their rotation while maintaining the Kimura grip, transitioning to side control or mount with the Kimura still secured

common_counters.counter: Opponent straightens their arm to prevent the figure-four grip
common_counters.your_response: Switch to an armbar attack or use your chest pressure to bend their elbow, then re-establish the Kimura grip with increased control

common_errors.error: Releasing chest pressure while attempting to secure the Kimura grip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes to their side or recovers guard, losing the dominant position entirely
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant downward pressure with your chest throughout the grip transition. Use your body weight, not just arm strength, to control the opponent

common_errors.error: Attempting the transition with insufficient control of opponent's far-side arm
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses their free arm to frame against your head or shoulder, creating space to escape
common_errors.correction: Control or pin the far-side arm first, either with your arm or by trapping it with your chest pressure before isolating the near-side arm

common_errors.error: Gripping the opponent's hand instead of their wrist for the figure-four
common_errors.consequence: Weak grip connection that allows opponent to slip their hand free and escape the submission
common_errors.correction: Grip the wrist with your thumb pointing toward their head, ensuring your grip is above their wrist joint for maximum control

common_errors.error: Sitting too far back too quickly when establishing the Kimura
common_errors.consequence: Loss of chest pressure allows opponent to bridge, turn, or escape to a better position
common_errors.correction: Shift your weight gradually, maintaining chest-to-chest contact until the Kimura grip is completely secure and your position is stable

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to keep their elbow tight to their body
common_errors.consequence: Cannot achieve the necessary angle to finish the submission or transition effectively
common_errors.correction: Use your chest and shoulder pressure to pry their elbow away from their ribs before attempting to feed their arm across their body

common_errors.error: Positioning your head too high near opponent's head instead of their hip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily escapes by bridging toward you or turning into your body
common_errors.correction: Keep your head low and positioned near their far hip to block their hip escape and maintain superior control

training_progressions.focus: Understanding North-South control and arm isolation mechanics
training_progressions.description: Practice establishing and maintaining North-South position without resistance. Work on isolating the near-side arm and feeding it across the opponent's body. Focus on proper chest pressure and weight distribution. Drill the movement slowly, emphasizing control and precision over speed.

training_progressions.focus: Mastering the figure-four Kimura grip and maintaining control
training_progressions.description: With light resistance, practice securing the Kimura grip from various North-South scenarios. Focus on grip placement, hand position, and connection strength. Partner provides minimal resistance to allow for technical refinement. Drill transitioning from grip to finish position.

training_progressions.focus: Executing the transition against moderate resistance and defensive reactions
training_progressions.description: Partner now actively defends by gripping their belt, attempting to turn, or framing. Practice reading and countering common defenses. Work on maintaining position through opponent's movements. Begin linking this technique with follow-up attacks and transitions.

training_progressions.focus: Applying the technique at full resistance in positional sparring
training_progressions.description: Start from North-South position in positional sparring rounds. Opponent uses full defensive effort to prevent the Kimura. Practice recognizing the optimal timing windows and chaining attacks when the primary technique is defended. Integrate into your overall top game strategy.

training_progressions.focus: Developing variations, feints, and high-level applications
training_progressions.description: Experiment with entries from different North-South variations, use the Kimura threat to set up other submissions, and develop your personal finishing mechanics. Practice against training partners of various sizes and skill levels. Incorporate into live rolling and competition scenarios.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of feeding the arm across the body, trap the opponent's arm on the near side with their palm facing up, then secure the Kimura grip in reverse. This variation is effective when the opponent defends the traditional grip by keeping their arm tight to their near side.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent successfully defends the cross-body feed by keeping their elbow tight to their ribs

variants_and_adaptations.description: Use the Kimura grip as a control handle to roll the opponent onto their side, then transition to back control while maintaining the Kimura grip. This creates a devastating position with both back control and a submission threat.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent begins to turn into you to defend the Kimura submission

variants_and_adaptations.description: From North-South, establish a crucifix position by trapping one arm with your legs while securing the Kimura grip on the other arm. This eliminates all of the opponent's defensive options and creates an inescapable control position.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When both of opponent's arms are exposed and you have excellent positional control

variants_and_adaptations.description: First establish the gift wrap control (opponent's arm trapped across their own body), then transition to the Kimura grip. This variation provides superior control during the grip transition phase.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent is defensively sound and you need additional control before attempting the Kimura grip

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary purpose of maintaining chest-to-chest pressure during the North-South to Kimura transition?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Chest-to-chest pressure serves multiple critical functions: it prevents the opponent from creating space to escape, limits their ability to bridge or turn effectively, keeps their shoulders pinned to the mat making arm isolation easier, and maintains your dominant position throughout the transition. Without constant pressure, the opponent can use bridging or turning movements to escape before you secure the Kimura grip.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why is controlling or neutralizing the opponent's far-side arm important before attempting the Kimura?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The far-side arm is the opponent's primary defensive tool from bottom North-South position. If left free, they can use it to frame against your head or shoulder, creating space to escape. They can also use it to grip their own belt or gi to defend the Kimura, or to post on the mat and bridge explosively. By controlling or pinning this arm first, you eliminate their most effective defensive options and ensure smooth execution of the Kimura transition.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the optimal head position during this transition and why?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Your head should be positioned low on the mat, near the opponent's far hip, throughout the transition. This position serves several purposes: it blocks their hip escape attempts by creating a barrier, it lowers your center of gravity making you harder to displace, it allows you to maintain better chest pressure, and it prevents them from turning into you effectively. Keeping your head too high near their head would make you vulnerable to bridges and escape attempts.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should you adjust your strategy if the opponent successfully grabs their own belt to defend the arm isolation?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When the opponent grabs their belt, direct attacks on the Kimura become inefficient. The best response is to switch your attack to their far-side arm with a choke, armbar, or other submission threat. This forces them to release their defensive grip to defend against the new threat. Once they release their belt grip, you can immediately return to the Kimura attack with a much higher success rate. This exemplifies the principle of creating defensive dilemmas.

knowledge_assessment.question: What mechanical advantage makes the Kimura from North-South particularly effective compared to other positions?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The North-South position provides several unique mechanical advantages for the Kimura: your entire body weight is distributed across the opponent's chest and shoulders, severely limiting their mobility and defensive options; their shoulders are flat on the mat, making it easier to manipulate their arm into the vulnerable position; you have superior leverage because you can use your chest, shoulders, and hips to apply pressure while their base is completely compromised; and the perpendicular angle of your body to theirs creates optimal leverage for the shoulder lock finish.

knowledge_assessment.question: Describe the proper hand positioning for the figure-four Kimura grip and explain why this specific grip is important?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The figure-four grip involves your near-side hand gripping the opponent's wrist with your thumb pointing toward their head, positioned above the wrist joint. Your far-side hand then reaches over their arm and grabs your own near-side wrist, creating a closed loop. This specific configuration is critical because it: creates a strong, unbreakable connection that the opponent cannot slip out of; allows you to control both the wrist and elbow simultaneously; provides the leverage necessary to manipulate the shoulder joint; and enables you to maintain control even under significant resistance. Gripping the hand instead of the wrist, or failing to create a proper closed loop, drastically reduces control and finishing ability.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent begins framing against your chest as you attempt to isolate their arm - how do you adjust?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When an opponent establishes frames, drive your chest pressure forward and angle your shoulders to slip past their forearms rather than fighting the frames directly. Alternatively, use the frame creation as a cue to attack the other arm or transition to a different attack angle. The key is to never stall against an established frame - either collapse it immediately with superior pressure and angles, or redirect to a different attack that exploits the arm position they've chosen. Their framing arm is now extended and potentially vulnerable to other attacks.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the optimal timing window to initiate the arm isolation for the Kimura transition?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing occurs when your opponent moves their arm to either push against you or attempt an escape. When they extend their arm to frame or bridge, it becomes temporarily separated from their body core, creating an isolation opportunity. Similarly, when they attempt to turn toward you, their near-side arm naturally comes across their body. The worst time to attempt isolation is when they're completely static with elbows tight to their ribs. Create reactions through pressure shifts or feigned transitions to generate the movement you need.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does your weight distribution change from initial North-South control to securing the Kimura Trap position?
knowledge_assessment.answer: In initial North-South, your weight is distributed forward with chest pressure across the opponent's upper body and head near their far hip. As you secure the Kimura grip, you gradually shift weight more laterally, moving perpendicular to their body while maintaining chest contact. Once the grip is secure, you can sit back slightly to create the finishing angle, but this must be gradual - sitting back too quickly before the grip is locked creates escape opportunities. The key is smooth, continuous pressure throughout the weight transition rather than sudden positional changes.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent straightens their arm as you attempt to establish the figure-four grip - what are your options?
knowledge_assessment.answer: A straightened arm presents both a challenge and an opportunity. First, you can use chest and shoulder pressure combined with your gripping hand to bend their elbow, forcing it into the required position. Second, you can immediately switch to an armbar attack since their extended arm is now perfectly positioned for that submission. Third, you can threaten the armbar to force them to bend their elbow defensively, then quickly transition back to the Kimura grip. The straight arm defense often backfires because it exposes them to alternative attacks.

knowledge_assessment.question: What indicators tell you the Kimura grip is secure enough to begin adjusting your body position for the finish?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The grip is secure when: your near-side hand has a firm wrist grip above their wrist joint with thumb toward their head; your far-side hand has a solid connection to your own wrist creating a complete loop; your elbows are tight to your body preventing the opponent from inserting their hand to break the grip; and you can feel that pulling their arm away from their body meets resistance from their shoulder rather than their grip slipping. Only when all these conditions are met should you begin shifting your body position, as premature movement with an insecure grip will result in losing the submission opportunity.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you chain from a failed Kimura attempt back to positional control without losing dominant position?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If the Kimura fails, immediately return your chest pressure to standard North-South control before the opponent can capitalize on any space created. Keep whatever grip you can maintain while resetting your base. From there, you can transition to side control for fresh attack angles, threaten the far-side arm with different submissions, or attempt to re-isolate the same arm with improved timing. The critical principle is never abandoning pressure - even if the submission fails, you should still be in dominant position ready to attack again.

safety_considerations: When training the North-South to Kimura transition, practitioners must exercise caution to prevent shoulder injuries. The Kimura places significant torque on the shoulder joint, and applying pressure too quickly or forcefully can result in serious injury including shoulder dislocation, rotator cuff tears, or labrum damage. Always apply the technique slowly and progressively, giving your training partner ample time to tap. When drilling, focus on control and positioning rather than forcing the finish. Partners should establish clear tap signals (verbal tap, physical tap with free hand, or foot tap if hands are trapped) before beginning. The person applying the technique must release immediately upon feeling any resistance or tap signal. When defending, do not wait too long to tap - protecting your training longevity is more important than ego. Instructors should closely supervise beginners learning this technique to ensure proper application and safety protocols are followed.
position_integration: The North-South to Kimura transition is a cornerstone technique in modern BJJ's top control system, bridging the gap between positional dominance and submission finishing. North-South position is typically achieved through transitions from side control, mount escapes, or successful guard passes, and represents one of the strongest control positions in grappling. From this position, the Kimura serves as both a high-percentage submission and a powerful control mechanism that opens multiple attacking pathways. When the direct Kimura finish is defended, practitioners can seamlessly transition to back control (rolling them with the Kimura grip), move to mount (using the arm as a handle), switch to armbars or chokes, or return to side control with superior arm control. This versatility makes the North-South to Kimura transition essential for any top game specialist. The technique also integrates into larger systematic approaches, particularly in submission-oriented games where practitioners chain submissions together. Understanding this transition is crucial for both offensive and defensive purposes - attacking practitioners must master the technique to capitalize on North-South opportunities, while defensive practitioners must understand the mechanics to defend intelligently and avoid injury. The position exemplifies the fundamental BJJ principle of using superior position to create submission opportunities while maintaining control and safety.
